props.title: The Hours
props.initialSlug: Three women, linked by Woolf's Mrs. Dalloway, face despair

sections.content: The Hours (2002) masterfully interweaves three women's stories across different time periods, all connected by Virginia Woolf's novel "Mrs. Dalloway." Director Stephen Daldry crafts a meditation on depression, creativity, and feminine identity that echoes Mrs. Dalloway (1997) and builds on the psychological complexity seen in Persona (1966). Nicole Kidman's prosthetic-nosed transformation into Virginia Woolf won her an Oscar, while Meryl Streep and Julianne Moore deliver equally nuanced performances that showcase the quiet desperation behind domestic facades.

sections.content: The film's innovative structure influenced later multi-narrative works like Babel (2006) and The Reader (2008). Philip Glass's hypnotic, pulsing score creates a dreamlike atmosphere that binds the three storylines while emphasizing their emotional isolation. Like Revolutionary Road (2008), it peels back the veneer of domestic contentment to expose raw psychological truth. The production design brilliantly distinguishes yet connects each era through subtle visual echoes.

Female-centered literary adaptations gained new momentum after The Hours' success. Films like Atonement (2007) and Little Women (2019) followed its lead in exploring women's interior lives with similar complexity. The Hours also paved the way for more nuanced LGBTQ+ representation in prestige drama, influencing works like Carol (2015) and Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019). sections.content: The Hours exemplifies how cinema can capture literary interiority through visual metaphor and performance. Like Orlando (1992), another Woolf adaptation, it uses period-specific details to illuminate universal themes. The film's treatment of mental illness avoided melodrama, setting a new standard followed by Melancholia (2011) and Still Alice (2014). Its exploration of creativity and madness recalls Sylvia (2003), while its examination of motherhood parallels Mother and Child (2009).
